```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(ggtypst)
```

## Why `ggtypst`?

ℹ️ One sentence summary: **`ggtypst`is for the moments when plain plot text is not expressive enough, but a full
external LaTeX workflow would be too heavy.**

---

Consider these scenarios: you have a scientific plot, and now you want to:

- show your title with multiple styles, for example, the first word is red and the rest is blue
- add some special characters like Greek letters in your axis titles
- add high-quality complex math expressions as annotations in the plot
- use the corresponding regression equation as the title of each facet

How would you achieve this?

- Base `ggplot2` text helpers are great for ordinary labels, but scientific and technical plots often need more than
  plain strings.
- You can use `expression()` in base R to add math. But its syntax is not natural and its functionality is limited.
- The package [`latex2exp`](https://www.stefanom.io/latex2exp/) helps you convert LaTeX math expressions to R
  expressions. But its functionality is also limited by `expression()`.
- The package [`ggtext`](https://github.com/wilkelab/ggtext) allows you to use Markdown and HTML tags to style your
  text. But it doesn't support complex styles and math.
- [`tikzDevice`](https://github.com/daqana/tikzDevice)/[`ggtikz`](https://github.com/osthomas/ggtikz) allows you to use
  LaTeX. But it is too complex to use and must rely on external TeX toolchains, which are very heavy.
- ...

So is there a simple, lightweight, easy-to-use solution? Yes, that's why `ggtypst` is here!

---

[Typst](https://typst.app) is a modern markup language and typesetting engine written in Rust. You can write source text
such as `*bold*`, `_italic_`, `#linebreak()`, or `$ sum_(i=1)^n x_i $`, and Typst turns it into polished rendered
output. It is fast, simple but powerful, solving these pain points perfectly and elegantly.

`ggtypst` uses Typst's Rust engine as the rendering backend and offers a series of functions to fit `ggplot2` workflow.
Typst lays the text out, and `ggtypst` draws the result with grid, just like `ggplot2` draws its own text.
With `ggtypst`, you don't need to leave your `ggplot2` workflow, don't need to rely on external LaTeX or Typst, and can
easily solve all the above use cases.

<details>
<summary>Click to see the code</summary>

```{r why-ggtypst, eval = FALSE}
eq_labels <- by(mtcars, mtcars$cyl, function(df) {
  fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = df)
  coef <- unname(coef(fit))

  sprintf(
    "hat(y) = %.1f %s %.1f x",
    coef[1],
    if (coef[2] < 0) "-" else "+",
    abs(coef[2])
  )
})

ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey50", size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 0.7,
    color = "#1D4E89"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(vars(cyl), nrow = 1, labeller = as_labeller(eq_labels)) +
  annotate_math_typst(
    r"(R^2 = 1 - sum(y_i - hat(y)_i)^2 / sum(y_i - macron(y))^2)",
    x = 3.5,
    y = 33.5,
    size = 10
  ) +
  labs(
    title = r"(#text(fill: red)[Scientific] #text(fill: blue)[plot text, math, and facet equations])",
    x = "Weight α (1000 lbs)",
    y = "Fuel economy η (mpg)",
    caption = "Smooth line formula: $y ~ x$"
  ) +
  theme(
    text = element_typst(size = 12, colour = "#102A43"),
    plot.title = element_typst(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_math_typst(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_typst(size = 9, colour = "grey50", face = "italic")
  )
```

</details>

```{r}
    "hat(y) = %.1f %s %.1f x",
    coef[1],

  )
})

ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey50", size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 0.7,
    color = "#1D4E89"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(vars(cyl), nrow = 1, labeller = as_labeller(eq_labels)) +
  annotate_math_typst(
    r"(R^2 = 1 - sum(y_i - hat(y)_i)^2 / sum(y_i - macron(y))^2)",
    x = 3.5,
    y = 33.5,
    size = 10
  ) +
  labs(
    title = r"(#text(fill: red)[Scientific] #text(fill: blue)[plot text, math, and facet equations])",
    x = "Weight α (1000 lbs)",
    y = "Fuel economy η (mpg)",
    caption = "Smooth line formula: $y ~ x$"
  ) +

```

## Installation

`ggtypst` requires R 4.3 or later. Regardless of how you install it, you don't need a separate local Typst or LaTeX
installation to use it.

### Install from pre-compile binary

Install `ggtypst` from R-universe first so you can use the prebuilt package and avoid compiling Rust locally. On
**Windows** and **macOS**, you can run:

```{r}
#| label: install-binary
#| eval: false
install.packages("ggtypst", repos = "https://yousa-mirage.r-universe.dev")
```

On **Ubuntu 24.04**, you should run:

```{r}
#| label: install-binary-ubuntu
#| eval: false
linux_binary_repo <- function(universe) {
  sprintf(
    "https://%s.r-universe.dev/bin/linux/noble-%s/%s/",
    universe,
    R.version$arch,
    substr(getRversion(), 1, 3)
  )
}

install.packages("ggtypst", repos = linux_binary_repo("yousa-mirage"))
```

### Install from source code

If you are on other Linux platforms, or you need the latest development version, you can install it from source:

```{r}
#| label: install-github
#| eval: false
devtools::install_github("Yousa-Mirage/ggtypst")
```

Because the GitHub installation builds the Typst backend in Rust, you need `rustc` (1.89 or later) and `cargo` on your
system to compile it. Particularly on Windows, you must use the `x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` toolchain.

## First plot

A quick example is like this:

```{r}
#| label: first-plot
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey50") +
  annotate_typst(
    typst_code = "*Hello from Typst!* #linebreak() $sum_(i=1)^n x_i$",
    x = 4.8,
    y = 32,
    size = 14,
    color = "#1D4E89"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "A first ggtypst plot",
    x = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
    y = "integral_0^1 x^2 dif x = 1/3"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_typst(
      size = 16,
      face = "bold.italic",
      colour = "#102A43"
    ),
    axis.title.y = element_math_typst(size = 14, colour = "#1D4E89")
  )
```

This shows the core usage of the package:

1. First, we use `annotate_typst()` to add a Typst label containing text and inline math.
   - `* ... *` marks bold text.
   - `#linebreak()` inserts a line break.
   - `$...$` marks inline math.
   - We specified the plot location, text size and color by other arguments.
2. Then, we want to render the title and axis titles with Typst.
   - We write a common title, and then render it with Typst through `element_typst()`.
   - We want to use a math expression as the y-axis title, so we write the Typst math source code in `labs()` and then
     use `element_math_typst()` to render it.

## When to use annotate, geom, and element

Use the three function families according to where the rendered content comes from.

| Function family | Best for                  | Typical use                                    |
| --------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `annotate_*()`  | one manually placed label | a callout, note, or equation                   |
| `geom_*()`      | one label per row of data | point labels, grouped labels, math annotations |
| `element_*()`   | theme text                | titles, subtitles, axis text, strips, legends  |

## R raw strings

Most Typst code is fine in an ordinary R string: `"*bold text*"` or `"$sum_(i=1)^n x_i$"` need no escaping, and many
examples in this article are written that way.

Two characters are special in ordinary R strings, though: `\` and `"` must be escaped as `\\` and `\"`. They are common
in LaTeX math (`\frac`, `\alpha`) and in Typst code that passes text in quotes (`#text(font: "Arial")`, or `"text"`
inside math). Introduced in R 4.0.0, R raw strings `r"( ... )"` take everything literally, so you can copy such code
unchanged:

```{r}
#| label: raw-strings
#| eval: false
# The same LaTeX formula as an ordinary string and as a raw string
"\\frac{a}{b}"
r"(\frac{a}{b})"

# Quotes inside Typst code
"$\"a text in math\" sum_(i=1)^n x_i$"
r"($"a text in math" sum_(i=1)^n x_i$)"
```

ℹ️ Use raw strings whenever the code contains `\` or `"`, which is almost always the case with LaTeX math. For
longer or copied code, they also save you from checking every character.

## Text, Typst math, and MiTeX math

`ggtypst` supports three related but different kinds of content.

### Typst markup content

Typst is a language for typesetting documents. It has two modes: the markup mode and the function mode. In markup mode,
you write plain text with Typst markup syntax, similar to writing Markdown. For more details, please see the [Typst
documentation](https://typst.app/docs/). It's very easy to learn and use.

Use `annotate_typst()`, `geom_typst()`, or `element_typst()` when the label is mostly text. For example:

```r
annotate_typst(
  typst_code = r"(*bold text*)",  # `*...*` means bold text
  x = 1,
  y = 1
) +
annotate_typst(
  typst_code = r"($a^2 + b^2 = c^2$)",  # `$...$` means inline math
  x = 2,
  y = 2
) +
annotate_typst(
  # In the line below, "Red text" is styled with `fill: red`, "default text" is styled with italic, and `+` is with default style.
  typst_code = r"(#text(fill: red)[Red text] + _default text_)",
  x = 3,
  y = 3
)
```

Yeah, actually you can write any legal Typst content in `typst_code`, including math, styled text, layouts, and
functions. You can even write a full Typst document in `typst_code`, as long as the source string is legal Typst
content. They will be directly rendered by Typst.

The one exception is files: `ggtypst` does not read files, so `#image("logo.png")`, `#read()`, `#include`, and
`#import` of a local file don't work.

### Native Typst math

You can use `*_math_typst()` when you want to write math directly. They are wrappers around `*_typst()` that use the
`typst_math_code` argument instead of `typst_code`.

```{r}
#| label: typst-math-example
#| eval: false
annotate_math_typst(
  typst_math_code = r"(sum_(i=1)^n x_i)",
  x = 1,
  y = 1
)
```

`$ ... $` or `$...$` will be automatically added around your math code to make sure it is rendered as a math expression.
The difference is, `$ ... $`, which is default, means display math, while `$...$` means inline math. You can use the
`inline` argument to control which to use.

Of course, you can also use `annotate_typst()` and write your math code in `$ ... $` or `$...$`. `*_math_typst()` are
just more convenient wrappers.

One more important benefit of Typst is that you don't need to have a math font installed on your system to render math
expressions. Typst has embedded the `New Computer Modern Math` font in binary, so you can render math anywhere and
anytime.

`New Computer Modern Math` is designed for print and has thin strokes, so formulas may look light at small sizes. If
they do, you can use a sturdier math font installed on your system with `math_family`, such as STIX Two Math:

```{r}
#| label: math-family-example
#| eval: false
annotate_math_typst(
  r"(sum_(i=1)^n x_i)",
  x = 1,
  y = 1,
  math_family = "STIX Two Math"
)

# Or for all theme text at once
theme(text = element_typst(math_family = "STIX Two Math"))
```

### MiTeX-backed LaTeX math

You can use `annotate_math_mitex()`, `geom_math_mitex()`, or `element_math_mitex()` if you are more familiar with LaTeX
math syntax or when your input is already in LaTeX. `ggtypst` converts LaTeX math into Typst math by
[MiTeX](https://github.com/mitex-rs/mitex) in the Rust backend. According to their documentation, this conversion is
stable and supports a wide range of LaTeX math syntax.

```{r}
#| label: mitex-example
#| eval: false
annotate_math_mitex(
  latex_math_code = r"(\frac{1}{2} + \sqrt{3})",
  x = 1,
  y = 1
)
```

## `annotate_*()`: one-off plot annotations

`annotate_*()` is the easiest place to start because it behaves like a normal manual annotation layer. Use this function
family when you just want to add one rich text note or math equation at a specific position.

```{r}
#| label: annotate-example
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65") +
  annotate_typst(
    typst_code = r"(Some plain text)",
    x = 2, # You must specify the x and y position manually
    y = 15
  ) +
  annotate_typst(
    typst_code = paste(
      r"(*Fuel economy* #linebreak())", # text with bold markup and line break function
      r"(#text(fill: rgb("#1D4E89"))[Typst text] +)", # text with fill color
      r"($integral_0^1 x^2 dif x = 1 / 3$)" # inline math
    ),
    x = 4,
    y = 33,
    size = 12,
    color = "#102A43"
  ) +
  annotate_math_mitex(
    latex_math_code = r"(\eta = \frac{mpg}{wt})", # LaTeX math code
    x = 5,
    y = 25,
    size = 14,
    color = "green",
    face = "bold"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

## `geom_*()`: data-driven labels

`geom_*()` turns Typst source strings into a true data layer. Each row gets its own rendered label and can map
aesthetics like `colour`, `angle`, and `face`. Use this family when:

- you have many labels to render
- labels come from rows in a data frame
- each label may have different styling
- you want Typst output to behave like other `ggplot2` geoms

```{r}
#| label: geom-example
labels <- data.frame(
  wt = c(2, 3, 5),
  mpg = c(33, 25, 15),
  label = c(
    r"(*Toyota Corolla* #linebreak() 33.9 mpg)",
    r"(*Fiat 128* #linebreak() nimble + efficient)",
    r"(*Maserati Bora* #linebreak() $v_8$ flagship)"
  ),
  colour = c("yellow", "#3A86A8", "#7A1E48"),
  face = c("italic", "bold.italic", "bold")
)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey80", size = 2) +
  geom_typst(
    data = labels,
    aes(wt, mpg, label = label, colour = colour, face = face),
    size = 12,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_colour_identity() + # this is needed for colour mapping
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

`geom_typst()` handles many labels well: each label adds under a millisecond to a PNG and about two milliseconds to a
PDF, less than with `ggtext::geom_richtext()`. For details, see [the benchmark
result](https://yousa-mirage.github.io/ggtypst/articles/benchmark.html). But you should still keep the number of labels
moderate anyway, so that the plot stays readable.

## `element_*()`: Typst in theme elements

`element_*()` is used to render the text of theme elements with Typst. By `element_*()`, you can place rich text,
special characters, and math equations in your plot titles, subtitles, axis titles, legend text, and facet strips.

*Imagine that your `ggplot2` title is a math matrix, while each facet label is the special regression equation!*

```{r}
#| label: element-example
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = r"(`ggplot2` + Typst-rendered theme text)",
    subtitle = r"(Titles and legends can use *Typst markup* directly)",
    x = r"($"X-axis title:" sum_(i=1)^n c_i$)",
    y = r"(\eta = \frac{mpg}{wt})", # LaTeX math is OK
    colour = r"(_*Cylinders*_)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_typst(size = 16, face = "bold", colour = "#102A43"),
    plot.subtitle = element_typst(size = 11, colour = "#486581"),
    axis.title.x = element_math_typst(size = 13),
    axis.title.y = element_math_mitex(size = 13, face = "bold"),
    legend.title = element_typst(size = 12),
    legend.text = element_typst(size = 10) # render legend labels with Typst
  )
```

You can also set an element on a group of elements, such as `axis.text` or `strip.text`, or on the root `text`
element to draw all of a plot's text with Typst. Every child element inherits it:

```{r}
#| label: element-root-text
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "*Fuel economy* by weight",
    subtitle = r"(Efficiency $eta = "mpg" / w$, with weight $w$ in 1000 lbs)",
    x = r"(Weight $w$)",
    y = r"(Miles per gallon)",
    colour = r"(*Cylinders*)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(text = element_typst())
```

Labels that come from the data, such as the legend keys, axis labels of a discrete scale, and facet strips, are then
Typst markup too. Characters such as `*`, `_`, `$`, `#`, and `@` in them take their Typst meaning; escape them with a
backslash (`\@`) if you want them as they are.

### Typst rules for a whole element or layer

The arguments cover the common text settings. For anything else Typst can do, you can give `preamble` Typst rules, such
as `#set` and `#show` rules, in `element_typst()` or `geom_typst()`. They apply to every label of the element or layer,
and come after the settings from the other arguments, so they can override them:

```{r}
#| label: preamble-example
#| eval: false
theme(
  text = element_typst(
    preamble = c(
      # A heavier math font, and slightly wider letter spacing
      r"(#show math.equation: set text(font: "New Computer Modern Math", weight: 450))",
      "#set text(tracking: 0.3pt)"
    )
  )
)
```

Like other element properties, an element inherits `preamble` from its parent unless it sets its own, which replaces
the parent's rather than adding to it. `preamble = ""` drops the inherited rules.

## Fonts and output devices

Typst's own fonts are built into `ggtypst`: Libertinus Serif for text and New Computer Modern Math for math. They are
always available, so your plots look the same on every computer. You can use `family` and `math_family` to choose any
other font installed on your system, for example to match the rest of your plot, to show Chinese or Japanese text, or
to get math that reads better at small sizes than the default (see [Native Typst math](#native-typst-math)).

If the family is not found, Typst warns and uses its default font. `typst_fonts()` lists the font families Typst can use;
use the names in its `family` column, which may differ from the names other software shows. `typst_fonts(detail = TRUE)`
also lists the weights and styles of each family.

For weights other than plain and bold, set `fontweight` (alias `weight`) to a number from 100 to 900 or to a name such
as `"light"` or `"semibold"`. It works in `annotate_typst()`, `geom_typst()` (also as a mapped aesthetic), and
`element_typst()`, so one setting can cover all theme text:

```{r}
#| label: fontweight-example
#| eval: false
theme(text = element_typst(family = "Helvetica Neue", fontweight = "light"))
```

Typst uses the closest weight the family has. For example, Libertinus Serif has three weights: regular (400),
semibold (600), and bold (700). So `fontweight = 300` looks like 400 and `900` like 700. A `fontweight` replaces the weight of a bold
`face` but keeps an italic one.

Variable fonts, which have one file whose weight can vary along an axis, follow `fontweight` too. Text in a variable font is always drawn as outlines.
A few old variable fonts, such as Skia on macOS, use non-standard axis values, and Typst then draws them in their heaviest style at any weight.
Set the axes yourself in the Typst code in that case, for example `#set text(variations: (wght: 1, wdth: 1))` for Skia's regular style.

`ggtypst` draws text the way the graphics device handles fonts best:

- On devices that rasterize or embed fonts, such as PNG files (`ragg` or `png()`), `cairo_pdf()`, `svglite`, and
  Quartz on macOS, text is drawn as native glyphs, exactly like `ggplot2`'s own text.
- `pdf()` and `postscript()` only refer to fonts by name. So on them, and on devices `ggtypst` does not recognize,
  text is drawn as outlines. Outlined text looks the same everywhere but cannot be selected or searched in a PDF; use
  `cairo_pdf()` to embed the real fonts instead.

Gradients, images, and color emoji are drawn as high-resolution images. See `?ggtypst-options` to change how text is
drawn or the resolution of those images.

## Next steps

From here, you can explore:

- the [function reference](https://yousa-mirage.github.io/ggtypst/reference/index.html) for `annotate_*()`, `geom_*()`,
  and `element_*()`, and `?ggtypst-options` for the drawing options
- the [benchmark](https://yousa-mirage.github.io/ggtypst/articles/benchmark.html) for how long plots take to draw
- the [contributing guide](https://yousa-mirage.github.io/ggtypst/CONTRIBUTING.html) if you want to understand the
  R/Rust architecture
- and practice `ggtypst` in your RStudio/Positron/VS Code
